verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, a psalm of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster. A psalm, David's own.
verses.directors_commentary: This line is the heading, and in the Hebrew Bible it counts as verse 1. That is why the KJV, which leaves it unnumbered as 'verse 0', stays one number behind from here on. The KJV's 'chief Musician' is a guess at a rare word: the root נצח means 'to be pre-eminent, to be lasting', and the participle probably names a leader or overseer of the temple music, as YLT's 'Overseer' keeps. 'Of David' (לדוד) may mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to the collection of' David. The old commentators tie the psalm to David's flight from Saul (Radak), a link the text itself never makes.

philological_notes.note: The participle of a verb meaning 'to excel, to be supreme'. As a heading it names the one who leads the performance; 'choirmaster' and 'overseer' are both attempts at an office we know only from these headings.
A song sung to a stringed accompaniment. The word marks the poem as music, not a private prayer.

verses.translation_literal: In you, YHWH, I have taken refuge; may I not be ashamed for ever; in your righteousness, rescue me.
verses.translation_dramatic: In you, LORD, I have run for shelter. Do not let me be shamed, not now, not ever. By your own righteousness, pull me clear.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker opens with the one fact on which the prayer rests: 'I have taken refuge' in you. The verb חסה pictures an animal or a person running under a rock or a wing, and it is a verb of trust acted out, not a feeling. 'Ashamed' is not embarrassment; in the Psalms shame is public defeat, the moment when the enemy's boast proves true and the one who trusted in a god is shown to have trusted in nothing. To ask 'let me not be ashamed' is to ask God to protect his own reputation as much as the speaker's life. The KJV's 'put my trust' is a pale rendering of a verb with physical movement in it; the ASV's 'take refuge' is closer. Last, 'in your righteousness' is not the KJV's neat 'deliver me in thy righteousness' in the sense of legal acquittal alone: the Hebrew צדקה is the covenant faithfulness that puts things right, and the speaker appeals to God's character, not his own record. Radak says so plainly: 'in your righteousness, and not in mine'. The same words open Psalm 71.

philological_notes.note: To flee for shelter, to seek cover. It is the psalter's verb for trust as movement toward a protector.
To be put to shame. It means the public reversal of fortune that shows a hope was in vain, not a private feeling.
God's own righteousness, here his faithfulness in setting things right. The speaker appeals to it instead of his own.

verses.translation_literal: Incline to me your ear, quickly rescue me; be for me as a rock of refuge, as a house of strongholds to save me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lean down to me. Bend your ear, and be quick, for I have no time. Be my rock, my high place, my house with walls too steep to climb; be the place where I am saved.
verses.directors_commentary: The first half is urgent speech: three commands in a row, 'incline', 'rescue', 'be'. 'Incline your ear' is a physical picture of a listener stooping to a speaker who is too weak or too far away, and Ibn Ezra notes that the Torah speaks 'in the language of human beings' here. The KJV's 'Bow down thine ear' and 'speedily' are fine. The second half stacks fortress words. צור is a crag or cliff face, and מעוז a place of refuge; 'house of strongholds' (בית מצודות) is a fortified house, a stronghold on a height, and Radak compares David's own 'stronghold' (1 Chronicles 11:16). After the verb 'be', the preposition ל means 'be to me as, become': the speaker asks God to become the thing he flees into. The KJV's 'for' renders that literally and is sound; YLT's 'Be to me for' does the same. The KJV's 'house of defence' is vaguer than the Hebrew, which names a house built to be a fastness. In a land of limestone ridges and caves, safety is high, rocky and hard to reach, which is why the images come as a pile. Rashi glosses מצודות with an Old French word for a fortress.

philological_notes.note: 'Stretch out, bend' the ear. An idiom for attentive listening, drawn from a person leaning toward a speaker.
A fastness, a mountain stronghold. The root also yields words for hunting and a hunter's net, so it carries the thought of a place where the hunted cannot be reached.

verses.translation_literal: For my rock and my stronghold are you; and for the sake of your name you will lead me and you will guide me.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you are my rock. You are my fortress. And so, for the sake of your own name, lead me; guide me, step by step.
verses.directors_commentary: Verse 3's wish becomes a statement: 'you ARE my rock and my stronghold', and Ibn Ezra notes that the two nouns answer the two in the previous verse. Then the request turns on 'for the sake of your name'. In the Hebrew world a name is reputation and character, so the speaker asks God to act to protect who he is known to be. Radak puts it: 'for your name's sake, not for mine'. The two verbs are different shades of the same motion. נחה is to lead on a way, and Ibn Ezra says that walking on a mountain is hard because of its height; נהל is to lead gently, 'slowly' in his word, as a shepherd leads a flock to water. The KJV's 'lead me, and guide me' flattens the pair into synonyms, and its 'therefore' adds a logical link the Hebrew does not mark: the Hebrew has 'and'. Rashi glosses תנחני with an Old French word for 'lead' and cites Exodus 32:34.

philological_notes.note: To lead along a road. Used of God leading Israel, as in Exodus 32:34.
To lead with care, at the pace of the weakest; a shepherd's word. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'slowly'.

verses.translation_literal: You will bring me out from a net which they hid for me, for you are my refuge.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bring me out of the net. They set it for me in secret, and they covered it well. Bring me out, for you are the place where I run.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a hunter's image. The net is a fowler's or hunter's snare, spread on the ground and covered so that the animal walks in without seeing it, and the same image of the hidden net returns across the Psalms for plots against the innocent. The verb טמן, 'hide, bury', is the word for a trap laid underground. The KJV's 'privily' is an archaism meaning 'in secret', and its 'pull me out' is stronger than the Hebrew, which is the mild 'bring me out'; it also turns the imperfect verb into a command, which is a fair reading of a form that here works as a plea. The ASV 'pluck' is equally heavy. The little word זו is poetic for 'which', and Ibn Ezra and Radak note that some read it as 'this net', as if the net were a known one; Radak says it was known to all. The last clause, 'you are my refuge', returns to the vocabulary of verse 3 (מעוז) and closes the first section of the psalm.

philological_notes.note: A poetic relative pronoun, 'which'. Radak notes that some take it as 'this' and so read 'this net'.
To hide, to bury; the word for a concealed trap. The subject is left open ('they'), which makes the enemy faceless.

verses.translation_literal: Into your hand I deposit my spirit; you have redeemed me, YHWH, God of truth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Into your hand I lay my spirit, as a man leaves what he treasures in a safe keeping. You have bought me back before, LORD, God who does not lie.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb אפקיד is a banker's word: to place something in someone's keeping, a deposit, with the duty of return. The KJV's 'commit' and the ASV's 'commend' are good, but they lose the sense of a deposit that the depositor expects to get back; Ibn Ezra notes that the very word explains why the next line speaks of God as 'of truth', for a deposit is safe only with a faithful keeper. 'My spirit' (רוח) is the breath, the life itself. Here the speaker hands his life over before the danger has passed, which is why Luke 23:46 later puts these words on the lips of Jesus on the cross, a use that the Hebrew psalm does not itself require. 'You have redeemed me' (פדיתה) is a perfect: in the past, God has bought this person back, as one pays a ransom for a slave or a firstborn. Rashi reads it as past rescue; Radak and Metzudat David read it as a perfect of certainty that stands for the future. 'God of truth' אל אמת is God who keeps faith, 'God who can be relied on', not the abstract 'truth' of the KJV.

philological_notes.note: To entrust, to leave in someone's care or deposit. Radak sets it against the enemies who lie in wait for the speaker's life: they ambush it and he deposits it with God.
To ransom, to buy back. A perfect verb that Radak and Metzudat David take to refer to the future, 'you will redeem me'.
'God of faithfulness'; אמת is what holds firm and can be relied on, not only what is factually true.

verses.translation_literal: I hate those who keep vanities of falsehood, but I, to YHWH I have trusted.
verses.translation_dramatic: I hate those who cling to empty things, to the idols and the lies. But I, I put my trust in the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: A sharp turn, and a contrast built into the grammar: 'I hate... but I'. The object of the hate is 'those who keep' (השמרים): 'keep' is the verb of a watcher, one who guards, observes or waits on something, as in Genesis 37:11, where Jacob 'kept' the matter in mind (Metzudat Zion). 'Vanities of falsehood' (הבלי שוא) is a double phrase for nothing: הבל is breath or vapour, the word Ecclesiastes uses for 'meaningless', and שוא is emptiness and deceit. The KJV's 'lying vanities' is a fair compromise but the 'regard' is mild. Rashi and Metzudat David read the phrase as those who wait for rescue from idols; Ibn Ezra and Radak as people who consult omens and astrologers. In all of these, the point is the same: the powers the neighbouring peoples trusted in were breath. The strongest verb, 'hate', is the language of covenant loyalty, in which to love one party is to reject the rival; it is not a private feeling. 'I trust to YHWH' with אל, 'toward', is a movement of the whole self; Radak compares Proverbs 3:5.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'breaths of emptiness'. The common biblical way of speaking of idols and false hopes, as in Jonah 2:9.
Those who keep, watch or wait upon. Metzudat Zion compares Genesis 37:11.

verses.translation_literal: I will rejoice and I will be glad in your covenant loyalty, that you saw my affliction, you knew, in the troubles of my self.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will cry out for joy. I will be glad in your steadfast love, because you saw me in my misery. You knew what I was in, the tight places of my soul.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood lifts: two verbs of joy back to back, אגילה and אשמחה, with the first a loud, bodily joy. The reason for it is not that the trouble has gone, but that God has seen it. 'Saw' and 'knew' are strong verbs in biblical Hebrew: God 'seeing' the affliction means acting on it, and the line recalls Exodus 3:7, 'I have surely seen the affliction of my people', as Radak points out, who also cites the same use of 'knew'. חסד is the KJV's 'mercy', which is too soft: it is covenant loyalty, the faithful love that binds one party to another in an agreement. The KJV's 'adversities' is fair, but it hides the root of צרות, which is צר, 'narrow, tight'. 'Troubles' are narrownesses, and that is the exact opposite of the 'wide place' (מרחב) in the next verse: the speaker has been in the tight places and God knew him there, and the next line sets his feet in the open. 'Soul' (נפש) is the whole living self, with its throat and its appetite.

philological_notes.note: Loyal love inside a relationship of obligation. 'Mercy' is too thin; 'covenant loyalty' keeps the sense of a bond.
'In the troubles of my self', literally the narrownesses. The plural of 'trouble' keeps the sense of tight places, the opposite of the 'wide place' (מרחב) that follows in the next verse.

verses.translation_literal: And you did not hand me over into the hand of an enemy; you made my feet stand in a wide place.
verses.translation_dramatic: You did not close me in the enemy's fist. You set my feet down on open ground, where there is room to move.
verses.directors_commentary: Two images, each the other's opposite. הסגרתני is 'you shut me up, you delivered me over', from the verb for closing a door or a gate; Rashi and Ibn Ezra tie it to the closing of a gate, the prisoner who is locked in and handed over. The KJV's 'shut me up' keeps this and is good. 'Into the hand of an enemy' is a standard phrase for being given over to someone's power. The reply is spatial: God has set the feet 'in a wide place' (מרחב). The KJV's 'large room' is an old English use of 'room' for space and now misleads; the Hebrew is open country, and it is the reverse of the narrow 'troubles' of the previous verse: tight places become a broad field. Ibn Ezra puts it simply: it means 'he goes where he likes'. The Hebrew has the feet 'made to stand', which is also a posture of security, of someone who is no longer on the run. Malbim reads it against Saul's encirclement of David, a link the psalm does not itself make.

philological_notes.note: To shut in, close up, and so to hand over. The same root as 'close a door'.
A broad, open place. A common biblical image for rescue as a movement from narrowness (צר) to breadth.

verses.translation_literal: Show me favour, YHWH, for it is tight for me; my eye has wasted away with grief, my self and my belly.
verses.translation_dramatic: Have pity on me, LORD, for I am hemmed in. My eyes are worn dim with grief, and my very self, and my belly with them.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm changes key. After confidence comes the complaint, and it opens with a play on the earlier word: 'for it is tight (צר) for me', the very root of 'troubles' two verses back, now said in the present tense. The speaker is again in the narrow place he thanked God for leaving. The verb עשש, 'to waste away, to decay', picks up three parts of the body in a list: the eye, the 'self' (נפש), and the 'belly' (בטן). The KJV's 'my soul and my belly' is truthful about the last word, but YLT and BBE soften it to 'body'. The Hebrew says the gut. In this idiom the belly is the seat of feeling, as with the guts of modern speech, and Radak and Ibn Ezra take it literally as the stomach that goes empty with hunger and grief. 'Grief' (כעס) is closer to 'vexation, provocation': a mixture of anger and sorrow caused by what others are doing. Rashi derives 'wasted' from the word for a glass lens, growing dim; Radak and Metzudat Zion from the moth, which eats cloth. 'Have mercy' is an old rendering of חנני; the Hebrew asks for grace, favour freely given.

philological_notes.note: To waste away. The old commentators link it to the moth (עש) that eats cloth, as Radak and Metzudat Zion do, or to a dimmed lens, as Rashi does; the sense is the same, a slow decay from within.
Vexation, anger mixed with sorrow, caused by the provocation of others. Ibn Ezra takes it as the enemy's anger toward the speaker.
The belly, as a seat of feeling. Radak takes the three terms (eye, self, belly) as the sight, the appetite and the gut.

verses.translation_literal: For my life has been finished in sorrow, and my years in groaning; my strength has stumbled through my iniquity, and my bones have wasted away.
verses.translation_dramatic: My life is used up in sorrow, my years in sighing. My strength gives way under my guilt, and my bones have rotted within me.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the grief becomes a measure of time. כלו is 'they are finished, used up', the verb for a supply that runs out, so that the whole of life is imagined as something poured away in sorrow and groaning. The pair 'life' and 'years' stretches the lament over the whole span. The next clause is the hardest: בעוני can be 'by my iniquity' or 'by my affliction'. The KJV and ASV choose 'iniquity', which is the usual sense of עון, the crooked deed and its consequence in one word. Ancient readers would hear a hint that the suffering has a cause in sin, and Radak calls it a figure: 'as a man says, through my sins this happened to me'. The psalm does not name the sin. 'Strength has stumbled' (כשל) is the verb for a person who trips on a bad road. The final clause repeats עשש from the previous verse, now applied to the bones, and the KJV keeps that echo: 'consumed' stands for it in both verses (31:9 'mine eye is consumed', 31:10 'my bones are consumed'), while YLT ('become old' only in the second) and BBE vary. In Hebrew thought, bones are the frame of the body, the part that cannot be seen to give way, so the line says the very structure of the self is rotting.

philological_notes.note: 'Iniquity', the wrong and its burden. Some take it as 'affliction' (the penalty of the iniquity); the psalm does not say what the wrong was. Radak reads it as a manner of speech.
The same verb as in the previous verse; here 'wasted away' is said of the bones, and Rashi explains it as rot, 'as if a moth had eaten them'.

verses.translation_literal: From all my opposers I have become a reproach, and to my neighbours exceedingly, and a dread to my acquaintances; those who see me in the street flee from me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before all who set themselves against me, I have become a thing of scorn; to my neighbours, a thing of scorn beyond measure; and to those who know me, a terror. They see me in the street and they run.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker's suffering is now social. In a village culture, honour is everything and the neighbours are the audience: to be a 'reproach' (חרפה) is to be a public insult, a story told against you. The verse moves in circles of closeness, from enemies to neighbours to 'acquaintances' (מיודעי, 'those who are known to me'), and each circle is worse than the last: strangers jeer, neighbours despise, and friends are afraid. 'Dread' (פחד) here is a thing others feel in his presence, as of someone who might draw trouble to them, which Radak and Metzudat David make explicit. The KJV's 'among all mine enemies, but especially among my neighbours' arranges the Hebrew into a comparison that is not quite in it, and BBE's 'shaking the head' adds a gesture the Hebrew does not have. The closing line is concrete and cruel: 'in the street' (בחוץ), literally 'outside', is the public space; those who see him there 'flee' (נדדו), the verb for wandering and fleeing. Ibn Ezra compares it to people avoiding the sight of a terrible illness. Jeremiah 20:10 knows the same pattern of 'terror on every side'.

philological_notes.note: Reproach, public insult and shame. In an honour culture it is a social wound, not just an unkind word.
'Those made known to me', my acquaintances; Metzudat Zion glosses it as those who know and love me, and compares Proverbs 7:4.
To flee, to wander off. Radak links it to the shaking of one who trembles, so the fleeing is also fear.

verses.translation_literal: I have been forgotten like the dead, from [the] heart; I have become like a vessel [that is] lost.
verses.translation_dramatic: I have been forgotten. Like the dead I have slipped out of every heart, and no one's thoughts turn my way any more. I am a thing mislaid and given up: a jar gone missing, and nobody out looking for it.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two pictures of being erased, played quietly: the dead, whom the living stop thinking of, and a household jar that has gone missing and is written off. In a village economy a lost pot was a small loss, soon replaced; that is the point. The speaker is not mourned, only dropped.

The KJV 'out of mind' is fair, but Hebrew says 'from the heart', and the heart is the seat of memory and attention. The KJV 'broken vessel' is a harmonizing guess: אֹבֵד is the participle of 'perish, be lost', the same verb as lost property in Deut 22:3, and Rashi and Radak both read an owner who has despaired of ever seeing it again. Play it as abandonment, not injury.

philological_notes.note: 'Lost, perishing', said of a vessel. Rashi stresses that the verb takes the lost thing as its subject: the object is lost from its owner, not destroyed by him. Hence 'lost' rather than 'broken'.
'From the heart': the heart is the organ of memory and attention in Hebrew, so being forgotten 'from the heart' is stronger than 'out of mind'.

verses.translation_literal: For I have heard [the] whispering of many: terror from round about; when they were seated together against me, to take my life they plotted.
verses.translation_dramatic: For I have heard it, the whispering of many. Terror on every side, and a ring of mouths closing round me. They sit down together, heads bent, against me; and the plan is not to bind me or shame me. It is to take my life.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene shifts from lonely neglect to a whisper campaign. דִּבָּה is quiet, damaging talk passed from mouth to mouth, the same word used of Joseph's 'evil report' about his brothers in Gen 37:2. 'Many' are speaking, and the speaker hears it secondhand, which is why it is so frightening: he cannot see the faces.

מָגוֹר מִסָּבִיב, 'terror from round about', is a stock phrase of dread; Jeremiah uses the same words of his own persecutors (Jer 20:10). It is a hammered-in image: no side is safe. The KJV 'fear was on every side' is acceptable but turns a noun phrase into a past-tense clause. בְּהִוָּסְדָם is 'when they were seated', as in a council that has formed; the KJV 'took counsel' gets the sense, and Rashi glosses it 'when they took counsel together'. Radak adds that the plotters want his life, not his enslavement: this is a death sentence, not a lawsuit.

philological_notes.note: Whispered slander, a bad report. Metzudat Zion links it to the 'report' of Gen 37:2; Rashi connects it with the root of 'moving the lips' in Song 7:10.
Niphal of יסד: 'when they were established / sat in council'. Ibn Ezra derives it from סוד, 'a council of intimates'; Metzudat Zion from 'foundation', a plan laid as a base.

verses.translation_literal: And I, on you I have trusted, YHWH; I said: My God [are] you.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I. I have set my whole weight on you, O LORD. I said it aloud, and I say it still: you are my God.
verses.directors_commentary:
A pivot in two words, וַאֲנִי, 'but I', placed against the 'many' of the last verse. The pronoun comes first for emphasis: they plot, but I trust. 'I said' is the verb of a stated commitment; Meiri hears it as a vow of loyalty, Radak as a statement of who is judge, 'you, not they'.

The KJV 'trusted in thee' blurs the preposition: Hebrew says עָלֶיךָ, 'on you', the language of leaning one's weight. The perfect tense בָטַחְתִּי is not only past: it is a settled stance, 'I have trusted and do'. Deliver it slowly, as a person catching their breath.

philological_notes.note: 'I have trusted, I rely'. With עַל it means leaning on something that bears the weight; here the perfect expresses a standing attitude.

verses.translation_literal: In your hand [are] my times; deliver me from [the] hand of my enemies and from my pursuers.
verses.translation_dramatic: My times are in your hand, every hour, good and bad. Then take me out of the hand of my enemies; pull me from the ones who run after me.
verses.directors_commentary:
One word of Hebrew, יָד 'hand', is deliberately repeated: my times are in your hand, so deliver me from the hand of my enemies. The play is on whose hand holds the speaker, and it is lost if one writes 'power' or 'grasp'.

עִתֹּתַי, 'my times', is not the abstract 'time' but the stretches and turns of a life, good and bad; Rashi says they pass 'by your decree'; Metzudat David, that they include both better and worse seasons. The KJV 'them that persecute me' softens the participle מֵרֹדְפַי: it is literally 'my pursuers', hunters chasing a runner, which fits a man on the run. BBE 'chances of my life' is closer in spirit than the KJV's flat 'times'.

philological_notes.note: Plural 'times': the seasons and turns of one's life, fortunate and unfortunate; the claim is that all of them are in God's hand, not fate's.
A participle, 'my pursuers': those who chase, as hunters or soldiers do.

verses.translation_literal: Make shine your face upon your servant; save me in your covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let your face shine on your servant. Turn your light my way, and save me, not because I have earned it, but because you are faithful.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Make your face shine' is the idiom of the priestly blessing (Num 6:25): a god, or a king, who is pleased with someone lets the face light up. Radak says the shining face just is salvation and success; Meiri hears it as a courtly image of a ruler who shows a bright face to someone he favors. The reverse, a hidden face, is the experience of the opening verses.

The KJV 'for thy mercies' sake' turns בְחַסְדֶּךָ ('in your חֶסֶד') into a reason; the preposition is 'in', and חֶסֶד is covenant loyalty, the obligation of faithfulness, not merely soft 'mercy'. The speaker also calls himself 'your servant', עֶבֶד, a word of status: the dependent of a master who is bound to look after him.

philological_notes.note: Loyal love inside a relationship, usually covenant faithfulness; 'mercy' loses the sense of obligation.
Idiom of favor from the priestly blessing; Radak equates the face's light with deliverance and success.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, let me not be ashamed, for I have called you; let [the] wicked be ashamed, let them be silent to Sheol.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, do not let me be shamed; I called on you. Let shame fall on the wicked instead, and let them go down silent into Sheol.
verses.directors_commentary:
Shame here is public: to be 'ashamed' is to have your hopes exposed as wrong before the people watching. The speaker's argument is simple: I called on you; if you do not answer, I am shamed. Rashi puts it plainly, that after calling on God it would not be fitting to be ashamed.

The verse swings the shame onto the enemies, with the same verb, אֵבוֹשָׁה / יֵבֹשׁוּ: the symmetry is the point. 'Let them be silent to Sheol' is a stronger phrase than the KJV's 'in the grave': the preposition is 'to', the movement is a descent into the underworld, and the silence is the silence of the dead. Radak glosses the verb as being cut off, with Jer 51:6 (אַל־תִּדַּמּוּ), and Rashi as 'be struck silent in death'. Scholars differ on דמם here, 'be silenced' or 'be destroyed'; the dramatic layer keeps both.

philological_notes.note: 'Be silent'; the commentators also take it as 'be cut off' (Radak with Jer 51:6, Metzudat Zion). In context it is the silencing of the grave.
The underworld, the place where the dead go, not a place of fire; Radak notes it may be read as the grave.

token_glosses.gloss: let them be put to shame

verses.translation_literal: Let them be dumb, [the] lips of falsehood, those speaking against [the] righteous [man] arrogant [talk], in pride and contempt.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let those lying lips go dumb, the lips that speak against the righteous, so hard, so haughty, so full of scorn.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker's wish moves from the enemies' fate to their mouths. The lips are the weapon: the slander of verse 14 is now cast as a body part that should be stopped. אָלַם is to be mute, the loss of speech, and the ill-wished muteness is a perfect answer to a whisper campaign.

עָתָק is the difficult word. The KJV 'grievous things' guesses at it; it means hard, arrogant speech, and Rashi gives two readings, one 'a thing that is not so, a slander' and one 'a hard, great thing'. Radak and Metzudat Zion take it as 'strong, hard', which suits 'pride and contempt'. 'Against the righteous' is singular, צַדִּיק, the type of the innocent person. Malbim reads it as God himself, which is a theological reading, not a plain one. The KJV 'proudly and contemptuously' converts two nouns into adverbs; the Hebrew has 'in pride and contempt' (בוּז, scorn).

philological_notes.note: Hard, arrogant speech; the root means 'move on, advance', so insolent talk that goes too far. Rashi records both 'a falsehood' and 'a great, hard thing'.
Contempt, scorn: looking down on someone as worthless.

verses.translation_literal: How great [is] your goodness which you have stored up for those fearing you, [which] you have done for those taking refuge in you, before [the] sons of humankind.
verses.translation_dramatic: How great is your goodness! You have laid it up in store for those who fear you, and you have worked it for those who take refuge in you, in plain sight of everyone.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens out. After the whispers and the threat, a cry of wonder, and two verbs for God's goodness: צָפַן, 'to store, hoard', as a farmer keeps grain in a granary; and פָּעַל, 'to work, to do', a goodness actually produced. The tension between the hidden store and the open deed is the verse's drama.

The commentators split over what is stored. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David say the stored good is the reward of the world to come; Radak adds that what is done 'before the sons of men' is the present rescue, visible to all. Ibn Ezra reads the open deeds as the answer to the arrogant speakers who 'know nothing' of the hidden store. Note also that 'those who fear you' and 'those who take refuge in you' are one group named twice. The KJV 'trust in thee' for חֹסִים misses the picture of a shelter: חָסָה is 'to run for cover'. The last phrase, נֶגֶד בְּנֵי אָדָם, can mean 'before them' (in their sight) or 'in front of them' in spite of them.

philological_notes.note: 'You have stored up, kept hidden': goods laid up for later; the same root returns in the next verse for hiding people.
Those who take refuge, as under cover from a storm or a pursuer; stronger than abstract 'trust'.

verses.translation_literal: You hide them in [the] hiding place of your face, from [the] plots of man; you store them in a booth, from [the] strife of tongues.
verses.translation_dramatic: You hide them in the secret place of your presence, away from the schemes of men. You tuck them into a shelter, safe from the quarrel of tongues.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse answers the 'strife of tongues' of verse 14 with two shelters. In the first, the face that shines in verse 17 becomes a hiding place: God's presence is a refuge, not a threat. In the second, a סֻכָּה, a leafy booth of branches such as farmers and shepherds throw up in the fields, a flimsy shelter that nonetheless gives shade; this is the same word used for the booths of Sukkot. The KJV 'pavilion' makes it sound grand.

מֵרֻכְסֵי is hard. The KJV 'pride of man' follows Radak, who derives it from 'to lift up' (the rings of the breastplate in Ex 28:28, 'the rough ground' in Isa 40:4); Rashi reads 'the alliances of the wicked, those who bind together against them'. 'Plots' catches both: knotted, bound-together schemes. The Targum has 'bands of men'. Ibn Ezra, followed by Malbim, reads 'the rough places'. The prepositions 'from' go with a concealing God, not an armed one: the picture is evasion, not battle. Note the repeated צפן, 'store/hide': what God stores is the same thing he conceals.

philological_notes.note: Disputed: 'conspiracies, bands' (Rashi), or 'pride, heights' (Radak, Metzudat Zion, from the verb 'to tie / to raise'). Ibn Ezra connects it with 'ridges' (Isa 40:4).
A booth of branches, a shelter for shade; the festival booth is the same word. Smaller and more fragile than 'pavilion'.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [be] YHWH, for he has made wonderful his covenant loyalty to me in a city of siege.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed be the LORD! For he has done a wonder with his faithful love toward me: in a city under siege.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood lifts to open praise, the first 'Blessed be' of the psalm. The wonder is placed in a city of מָצוֹר. The word means 'siege' or 'bulwark'; the KJV 'strong city' reads it as a fortified town, while Rashi names the siege exactly: Keilah, where Saul said he had shut David in 'a city of gates and bars' (1 Sam 23:7). Radak reads it figuratively: I was as safe as in a walled city. The Hebrew is deliberately ambiguous, a city being besieged and a city that is a fortress; keep the ambiguity.

הִפְלִיא is the verb of wonders, used of the acts that surpass ordinary explanation; the KJV 'shewed me his marvellous kindness' reads it as a showing, but the verb says that God made his loyalty wonderful, an act as much as a display.

philological_notes.note: 'City of siege' or 'fortified city'. Rashi: Keilah, besieged by Saul; Radak: 'as if I were in a walled city'.
Hiphil of פלא: 'to do something wonderful', set apart from the ordinary.

verses.translation_literal: And I, I said in my haste: I am cut off from before your eyes; yet you heard [the] sound of my supplications when I cried for help to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I, I said it in my panic: cut off! Cut from before your eyes! But you heard. You heard the sound of my pleading, the moment I cried out to you.
verses.directors_commentary:
A confession, with a turn. The speaker admits he doubted: in חִפָּזוֹן, the headlong haste of a man running for his life, he thought God had stopped looking at him. Rashi and Radak tie this to 1 Sam 23:26, where David 'was hurrying to get away from Saul' while Saul's men were closing in; Malbim has the same scene.

נִגְרַזְתִּי occurs only here. Rashi derives it from גַּרְזֶן, 'axe', so 'I am hewn off like a tree', a violent picture; the KJV 'I am cut off' keeps that. The structure is a hinge: 'I said ... yet you heard'. אָכֵן is the surprised 'indeed, in truth'; the KJV 'nevertheless' mutes the astonished correction. The scene hangs on the contrast of the two verbs, 'I said' in fear, 'you heard' in fact. The KJV 'cut off from before thine eyes' is faithful; its 'in my haste' misses the physical sense of flight in the verb.

philological_notes.note: Found only here; Rashi and Radak derive it from גַּרְזֶן 'axe': to be hewn off. Menahem, Rashi reports, takes it as 'driven out' like Jonah 2:5.
A particle of surprised confirmation, 'but in fact, truly'; it reverses the speaker's despairing guess.

verses.translation_literal: Love YHWH, all his faithful ones! [The] trustworthy YHWH [is] guarding, and [he is] repaying upon [the] excess [of the] doer [of] pride.
verses.translation_dramatic: Love the LORD, all you who are his own. The faithful, the LORD keeps safe. And the one who does his work in pride? The LORD pays him back, and pays him back in full, to the last measure.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here from private prayer to public command. The singer, saved from the 'vessel lost' of v. 13, now faces the congregation and speaks to them as a man with a story to prove. Play it as testimony, not sermon: 'look what he did for me, so love him.' The command to 'love' is less common than 'fear', 'trust' or 'praise'; the verb carries the loyalty of a covenant partner, not a mood.

The KJV 'saints' has gone churchy: chasid (חָסִיד) are the covenant-loyal, those who answer hesed with hesed, not the sanctified dead. Its 'faithful' for emunim is fair, but it flattens a contrast the Hebrew sets up: YHWH guards the trustworthy, the people who hold steady, and pays the arrogant 'upon excess'. The phrase 'al yeter is notoriously hard, and the KJV's 'plentifully' smooths over a real dispute. Rashi lists measure-for-measure (the arrow shot along the bowstring), rope against rope, and yeter as a word for pride itself; Ibn Ezra reads 'the remainder of the proud'. The simplest sense is repayment to the full, over and above, so that the proud do not merely lose, they overpay. Note too that 'doer of pride' (oseh ga'avah) is concrete: pride here is something done, a deed, not a feeling. That is why the KJV 'proud doer' is close but loses the stress on the act. Keep the grammar too: 'guarding' (notser) and 'repaying' (meshallem) are both participles, so God is caught in the act, continuously, on both sides of the ledger.

philological_notes.note: 'The trustworthy, the steady ones', plural of a rare adjective from the root of 'amen' and 'firm'. It echoes Ps 12:2 'the faithful vanish from among men', a contrast the singer is answering: the faithful are not lost, God is guarding them.

Literally 'upon excess / remainder'. Yeter also means a bowstring or cord, which is how Rashi gets 'measure for measure', and Rashi's last reading takes it as pride itself (Isa 15:7). Most take it as 'abundantly, to the full'.

verses.translation_literal: Be strong, and let your heart be firm, all [you] who wait for YHWH!
verses.translation_dramatic: Be strong. Let your hearts grow firm, every one of you who waits for the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last line of the psalm, and it is quiet. After twenty-four verses of panic, slander, hiding and rescue, the singer ends not with his own voice but with a blessing for everyone still in the dark. The verb 'wait' (yachal) means to hold on in hope, a rope-like tension; it is not idle waiting. The two imperatives are a pair: 'be strong' is yours to do, 'let your heart be firm' is a wish that lands on the body's centre. Say it low and steady, as someone who has been where the listener is, and remembers being the vessel [that was] lost.

The KJV 'Be of good courage, and he shall strengthen your heart' adds a subject, 'he', that the Hebrew lacks. The verb is a jussive, 'may it be firm', with 'heart' as its subject, and the KJV turns that into a divine promise. It is a pious guess and the Targum shares it, but the Hebrew leaves the agent open, and that openness suits the ending. Note also that 'heart' is levav, the full, doubled form, and not the shorter lev; the doubling gives the word a heavier, whole-person sound. The ASV 'let your heart take courage' is closest.

philological_notes.note: A jussive in the causative stem: 'and let it be strong' or 'and may [he] make strong'. The Hebrew form fits 'let your heart take courage' as well as the KJV's 'he shall strengthen'; the agent is not stated.
'Those who wait / hope', a participle of the verb of patient expectation, used of those who keep trust while the answer has not come.
